He remained imprisoned through at least September 1960; the exact release date remains unresolved.

profiles.name: John Juhn
profiles.description: John Juhn was a Korean independence activist, printer, editor, and co-owner of the Los Angeles newspaper Korean Independence. Immigration authorities arrested him in May 1955 and ordered him deported to South Korea on the claim that he had entered the United States without inspection in 1920. Supporters won a stay because of the danger posed by the Syngman Rhee government. Juhn and his wife Anna Song later left for North Korea through Czechoslovakia, but North Korean authorities denied them entry. The reviewed record does not establish exact custody endpoints after his arrest.
profiles.finding: Korean Independence research and historical scholarship found; reject contemporary director Joseph Juhn.

profiles.name: Sang Ryup Park

Immigration authorities ordered him deported on November 29, 1951 and took him into custody. A federal court ruled on May 9, 1952 that the government’s conclusion that he would not face political persecution was unsupported, enjoined deportation to South Korea, and subsequently ordered his release. The precise release date has not been established.

profiles.name: Augustus J. Johnson
profiles.description:
Augustus J. Johnson was a New York City subway motorman and an official of the Motormen's Benevolent Association, jailed in connection with the transit strike that began on December 9, 1957. His exact identity remains incompletely verified.

A contemporary Associated Press report states that FOUR association officials began serving previously suspended ten-day jail sentences after the strike started. THE ARTICLE DOES NOT NAME THE FOUR. His individual participation and his admission date are therefore probable rather than documented, and the ten-day sentence is recorded here as group evidence rather than as his own established term.

His canonical full identity, vital dates, arrest and original sentencing dates, the charge, the jail, the exact custody interval, his office in the association, the later outcome and a verified portrait are all unresolved. Cornell's Amsterdam News archive lists one print under "Johnson, A.J.", but it has not been shown to depict this man.
profiles.query: "Augustus J. Johnson" Motormen Benevolent photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Canonical identity remains unverified; reject1853-1878 namesake.

profiles.name: Albert E. Perry Jr.
profiles.description: Dr. Albert E. Perry Jr. was vice-president of the Union County NAACP in Monroe, North Carolina, and a close ally of Robert F. Williams. After helping lead a campaign to desegregate Monroe’s municipal swimming pool, he was prosecuted for performing an abortion in a case the NAACP denounced as retaliation for his civil-rights work. A retrial produced a two-to-three-year sentence, and Perry ultimately served eleven months at Caledonia Prison Farm.

profiles.name: Eugene Levin
profiles.description: Eugene Levin was a physician drafted into the Army under the Doctors Draft Law and denied a commission after invoking the Fifth Amendment on a loyalty questionnaire. He received an honorable discharge in June 1954. The case involved compulsory military service rather than jail or prison confinement.

profiles.description: Lieutenant Leon A.
